artiest/george-fenton.text:
George Fenton, born George Richard Ian Howe on 19 October 1949 in Bromley, Kent, was an English composer of film and television music. He had guitar lessons at the age of eight and studied organ at school with Peter Whitehouse, but never went to a conservatoire. In 1968 he appeared in Alan Bennett's first West End play, Forty Years On. He worked as an actor and musician and had a record deal with MCA. His 1969 cover of The Beatles' Maxwell's Silver Hammer became a big hit in Sweden.

In 1974 he received his first major commission: the music for the Royal Shakespeare Company's Twelfth Night. In the 1970s and early 1980s he wrote a great deal for the theatre, often with the director Peter Gill, and for the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre. Then came film. He wrote the music for Gandhi in 1982, Cry Freedom in 1987, Dangerous Liaisons in 1989, Groundhog Day, The Fisher King, You've Got Mail, Sweet Home Alabama and Hitch. He often worked with directors such as Richard Attenborough, Nora Ephron, Stephen Frears and Ken Loach.

Fenton also wrote the music for David Attenborough's natural history documentaries, such as Planet Earth, Frozen Planet and Wild Isles. He received five Oscar nominations and several Ivor Novello, BAFTA, Golden Globe, Emmy and BMI awards. He was one of the few songwriters and composers to be made a Fellow of the Ivors Academy.
artiest/george-fenton.listen: Listen to his music for Planet Earth and notice how the music carries the images of nature. Ask yourself what images you would expect with it if you did not know the film.

artiest/george-frideric-handel.text:
George Frideric Handel, christened Georg Friedrich Händel, was a German-British Baroque composer known for his operas, oratorios, anthems, concerti grossi and organ concertos. He was born in 1685 in Halle, the same year as Johann Sebastian Bach and Domenico Scarlatti, and died on 14 April 1759. His father was a prominent barber-surgeon at court. Handel spent his early years in Hamburg and Italy and settled in London in 1712, where he became a British subject in 1727.

He was strongly influenced by the central German choral polyphonic tradition and by the Italian Baroque. In London he set up three commercial opera companies to supply the English nobility with Italian opera. In 1737 he suffered a physical breakdown, changed course and, with choral works in English, turned to the middle classes. After his success with Messiah in 1742 he never wrote another Italian opera. Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks remain popular. Zadok the Priest, one of his four coronation anthems, has been heard at every British coronation since 1727.

Handel brought Italian opera to its highest development and created the English oratorio and the organ concerto. He died a respected and wealthy man and was given a state funeral in Westminster Abbey. Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven admired his music, and since the middle of the twentieth century interest has grown. The musicologist Winton Dean called him a great composer and a dramatic genius of the first order.
artiest/george-frideric-handel.listen: Listen to Zadok the Priest and notice the role of the choir and the orchestra. This piece has been heard at every British coronation since 1727.

artiest/george-gershwin.text:
George Gershwin was born in New York in 1898 and died in 1937 in Los Angeles of a brain tumour. He was 38. Gershwin wrote songs for Broadway and Hollywood, but also music for the concert hall and an opera. He is important because he linked the world of Tin Pan Alley, jazz and classical music.

At fifteen he left school and became a song plugger at the music publisher Jerome H. Remick: he played new songs to customers. His first big hit was Swanee (1919), sung by Al Jolson. Most of the lyrics were written by his older brother Ira. The bandleader Paul Whiteman asked him for a piece for a concert with his jazz orchestra. This is how Rhapsody in Blue came about, first performed in New York in 1924, which combines classical forms with sounds from jazz. The famous opening clarinet glissando was thought up by Whiteman's clarinettist Ross Gorman during a rehearsal. Later came An American in Paris (1928), the musical Girl Crazy (1930) with I Got Rhythm, and the opera Porgy and Bess (1935), with the song Summertime.

The chords of I Got Rhythm were used so often in jazz that they got a name of their own: rhythm changes. Bebop musicians wrote new melodies over them, such as Anthropology (1946) by Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie. Summertime became one of the most recorded jazz standards; Billie Holiday already had a hit with it in America in 1936. Porgy and Bess was at first not a commercial success, but is now regarded as one of the most important American operas of the twentieth century.
artiest/george-gershwin.listen: Listen to Anthropology by Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and sing I Got Rhythm along in your head: the melody is new, but the chords under the solos are Gershwin's.

artiest/george-harrison.text:
George Harrison was born on 25 February 1943 in Liverpool, the youngest of four children. His mother supported his love of music. In 1958 he joined The Quarrymen, John Lennon's group that later became The Beatles. There he first played lead guitar. His early models included Carl Perkins, Chet Atkins and Chuck Berry.

Lennon and McCartney wrote most of the songs, but almost every Beatles album included at least one song by Harrison, such as Taxman, While My Guitar Gently Weeps, Something and Here Comes the Sun. From 1965 he pulled the group towards folk rock and Indian classical music. He got to know the sitar on the set of the film Help! and played that instrument on a series of Beatles songs. In 1967 he also introduced the band to Transcendental Meditation. After the break-up of The Beatles he released the triple album All Things Must Pass (1970), with his biggest hit My Sweet Lord.

In 1971 he organised the Concert for Bangladesh with the Indian musician Ravi Shankar, a forerunner of charity concerts such as Live Aid. He founded the record label Dark Horse Records and a film company that produced Monty Python's Life of Brian (1979). In 1988 he formed the supergroup Traveling Wilburys with, among others, Bob Dylan and Tom Petty. Harrison was known as the quiet Beatle, but his interest in Eastern music left a clear mark on Western pop. He died of cancer in 2001, aged 58.
artiest/george-harrison.listen: Listen to My Sweet Lord (1970). Notice the gliding slide guitar that sings between the lines: that sound became the hallmark of Harrison's solo work.

artiest/george-kooymans.text:
George Kooymans was born on 11 March 1948 in The Hague. In 1961 the thirteen-year-old started a band with his neighbour Rinus Gerritsen. They first called themselves The Tornados, but when it turned out that a British group with that name had just had a hit, it became The Golden Earrings. In 1965 the breakthrough came with the first single Please Go. Shortly afterwards the singer Barry Hay joined, and in 1970, with the drummer Cesar Zuiderwijk, the line-up was complete that would stay together for fifty years.

Kooymans played guitar, sang and wrote most of the music and lyrics of what later became Golden Earring. The band became world famous with Radar Love (1973), Twilight Zone (1982) and When the Lady Smiles (1984). Twilight Zone, written by him, became the group's only top ten hit on the American Billboard Hot 100. Golden Earring had almost thirty top ten hits in the Netherlands and made 25 studio albums.

Kooymans also wrote and produced for others. He launched the singer Bojoura, discovered Earth and Fire and wrote their hit Seasons. Later he also wrote the Kinderen voor Kinderen hit Vuur en Vlam. From 2017 to 2023 he made three albums with Henny Vrienten and Boudewijn de Groot as the Dutch-language supergroup Vreemde Kostgangers. In February 2021 he announced that he had ALS and stopped making music, after which Golden Earring ceased to exist. He died in July 2025, aged 77.
artiest/george-kooymans.listen: Listen to Twilight Zone (1982). Notice Kooymans's tight, menacing guitar riff and how the music conjures up the tension of a spy story, with a long instrumental middle section.

artiest/george-lewis.text:
George Lewis, born Joseph Louis Francois Zenon, was an American jazz clarinettist, born on 13 July 1900 in New Orleans and died on 31 December 1968. He became best known in his last decades. Through his mother he had a Senegalese great-great-grandmother, and her family long preserved knowledge of the language and customs of Senegal. In the 1920s he formed the New Orleans Stompers and worked with, among others, Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit and Kid Rena. He also played in the Eureka Brass Band and the Olympia Orchestra. In the 1930s he played with Bunk Johnson, De De Pierce and Billie Pierce.

Because he earned too little as a musician, he loaded and unloaded ships on the Mississippi. In 1944 he was injured when a heavy container nearly crushed him. During his recovery his friends, the banjo player Lawrence Marrero and the bassist Alcide Pavageau, came to his bedside with their instruments. Bill Russell recorded their improvisation, Burgundy Street Blues, which became Lewis's trademark. Until 1946 he played in Bunk Johnson's band, with which he went to New York and recorded for Decca and Victor. After Johnson's departure Lewis took over the leadership.

His albums include Jazz Funeral in New Orleans from 1953, George and the Vikings from 1959 and Jazz at Preservation Hall 3 from 1963. He also recorded in Japan and with Papa Bue's Viking Jazzband.
artiest/george-lewis.listen: Listen to Burgundy Street Blues and notice the tone of his clarinet and the simple accompaniment. The piece came about during his recovery, with a few friends at his bedside.

artiest/george-m-cohan.text:
George M. Cohan was born in 1878 in Providence, Rhode Island, the son of Irish Catholic parents. His parents travelled around as vaudeville performers, and George was on stage as a baby. At eight he played the violin, and then he danced. With his father, mother and sister he formed the family act The Four Cohans, which toured America from 1890. As a teenager he was already writing sketches and songs for the group, and in 1893 he sold his first songs to a publisher.

His first big success on Broadway was the 1904 musical Little Johnny Jones, which included Give My Regards to Broadway and The Yankee Doodle Boy. After that he wrote, composed and produced dozens of shows, and often appeared in them himself. In all he published more than three hundred songs, including You're a Grand Old Flag and Harrigan. His song Over There became the most popular American song of the First World War. In the years before that war he was called the man who owned Broadway.

Cohan was one of the most important songwriters of Tin Pan Alley. His songs stand out for their catchy melodies and clever lyrics, and they are often proud and patriotic. He is regarded as the father of American musical comedy. His life was filmed in Yankee Doodle Dandy (1942), the year in which he died. In 1968 the musical George M! followed. In Times Square in New York there is a statue of him.
artiest/george-m-cohan.listen: Listen to Over There or Give My Regards to Broadway. Notice how short and catchy the chorus is, so that anyone can sing along after hearing it once: that is how a Tin Pan Alley song worked.

artiest/george-martin.text:
George Martin was born in 1926 in north London. When he was six a piano came into the house, and he taught himself to play. As a teenager he played in a small dance band. After his service in the navy he studied piano and oboe at the Guildhall School of Music. In 1950 he joined the record company EMI, and in 1955 he became head of the small label Parlophone. There he produced classical music, jazz and above all comedy records, including with Peter Sellers and Spike Milligan.

In 1962 he had The Beatles audition, after they had been turned down by Decca. It was the start of a collaboration that lasted until the end of the group. Martin had a classical training, whereas the Beatles had little musical schooling. He wrote most of the orchestral and string arrangements and played piano or keyboards on many tracks. On Eleanor Rigby the Beatles only sing, and the accompaniment is a string arrangement by Martin. Together with the engineers at Abbey Road Studios they were always searching for new sounds, as on Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967). That is why he was called the fifth Beatle.

In 1965 Martin started his own production company. After The Beatles he worked with, among others, Paul McCartney, America, Kate Bush and Jeff Beck, and wrote music for the Bond film Live and Let Die. In 1997 he produced Elton John's Candle in the Wind. He produced thirty number 1 hits in Britain and was knighted in 1996. Martin showed how important a producer can be to the sound of a band. He died in 2016.
artiest/george-martin.listen: Listen to Eleanor Rigby by The Beatles and notice the accompaniment. Hear that there is no guitar, bass or drums, only strings. Hear how they provide the rhythm and the tension underneath the vocals.

artiest/george-michael.text:
George Michael, born Georgios Kyriacos Panayiotou on 25 June 1963 in East Finchley, was an English singer, songwriter and producer. He died on Christmas Day 2016 of heart disease. In 1981 he formed the pop duo Wham! with Andrew Ridgeley. In 1984 he took part in Band Aid's Do They Know It's Christmas? and in 1985 he performed at Live Aid. His first solo album Faith from 1987 won a Grammy for Album of the Year. Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1 from 1990 followed, then Older from 1996, Songs from the Last Century from 1999 and Patience from 2004.

Michael had ten number 1 hits on the American Billboard Hot 100 and thirteen on the British chart. His best-known songs include Careless Whisper, A Different Corner, Faith, Father Figure, One More Try, Freedom! '90, Jesus to a Child and Fastlove. The Radio Academy named him the most-played artist on British radio from 1984 to 2004. He was praised for his songwriting, his singing and his visual presentation.

In 1998 he came out openly as gay, and later he campaigned for LGBTQ rights and for charities fighting HIV and AIDS. In 2006 he began the 25 Live tour, which lasted three years, and in 2012 he gave his last concert at Earls Court in London. In 2023 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted him.
artiest/george-michael.listen: Listen to Faith and notice the voice. Can you hear that George Michael is no longer singing here as a member of Wham!, but as a solo singer?

artiest/george-russell.text:
George Russell was born in 1923 in Cincinnati, Ohio, and grew up as an adopted child. He sang in a church choir and heard the big bands that played on the Ohio river steamers. At the age of seven he was already on stage with Fats Waller. He began as a drummer and played in Benny Carter's band. When he was called up during the Second World War, he turned out to have tuberculosis. In hospital a fellow patient taught him the basics of music theory. He then moved to New York, where he belonged to a group of young innovators around Gil Evans, with, among others, Miles Davis, Charlie Parker and Gerry Mulligan.

His first famous piece he wrote for Dizzy Gillespie's orchestra: Cubana Be, Cubana Bop (1947), in which bebop and Afro-Cuban music come together. During a second long stay in hospital he worked out his theory, which he published in 1953 as Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization. It was one of the first theories of harmony to take jazz rather than European music as its starting point. His modal ideas influenced Miles Davis and John Coltrane in the recording of Kind of Blue. With his own groups, with, among others, Bill Evans, he made albums such as New York, N.Y. (1959) and Ezz-thetics with Eric Dolphy.

From 1964 to 1969 Russell lived in Scandinavia, where he worked with young musicians such as Jan Garbarek and Terje Rypdal and experimented with electronic tape. Afterwards he taught for years at the New England Conservatory in Boston. His music was often complex and layered. He died in 2009.
artiest/george-russell.listen: Listen to Cubana Be, Cubana Bop by Dizzy Gillespie's orchestra. Notice how the Cuban percussion of Chano Pozo and the bebop horns come together in a single piece.

artiest/george-shearing.text:
Sir George Albert Shearing was a British jazz pianist and composer, born on 13 August 1919 in Battersea in London and died on 14 February 2011. He was the youngest of nine children and was born blind. His father delivered coal, and his mother cleaned trains in the evenings. At three he began learning the piano, and later he took formal lessons at a school for the blind. He played in a pub in Lambeth, in a band of blind musicians, and was influenced by records by Teddy Wilson and Fats Waller. He began recording in 1937 together with Leonard Feather.

In 1940 he joined Harry Parry's band, and around 1942 Stéphane Grappelli asked him to join his group, with which he toured from 1943. Later he emigrated to the United States, where his harmonically rich style, a blend of swing, bop and modern classical influences, caught on. In 1949 he formed the first George Shearing Quintet, with, among others, the vibraphonist Margie Hyams, the guitarist Chuck Wayne, later replaced by Toots Thielemans, the bassist John Levy and the drummer Denzil Best. The single September in the Rain sold more than 900,000 copies in the United States alone.

Shearing wrote more than three hundred songs, including the jazz standards Lullaby of Birdland and Conception. He had albums on the Billboard charts in the 1950s, 1960s, 1980s and 1990s, such as Beauty and the Beat! from 1959 and Sassy Meets Shearing! from 1962. The writer Jack Kerouac heard him at Birdland and described his playing in On the Road.
artiest/george-shearing.listen: Listen to Lullaby of Birdland and notice how the piano plays melody and chords at the same time. Can you also hear the vibraphone and the guitar joining in the sound of the quintet?

artiest/george-telek.text:
George Telek Mamua, usually called simply Telek, is a musician and singer from Papua New Guinea. He was born in 1959 in the village of Barovon near Kokopo in East New Britain province and is one of the few singers from his country with an international following. He sings in his mother tongue Kuanua and in Tok Pisin. Many of his songs are in three-part harmony, a feature of the Tolai, the people to whom he belongs.

Telek used to sing with various bands in Papua New Guinea, above all with the Tolai group Painim Wok, where he was lead singer. In 1989 he met David Bridie of the Australian band Not Drowning, Waving. Together they recorded the album Tabaran, which came out in 1990 and was nominated for an ARIA Award in 1992. His first solo album Telek from 1997 won an ARIA Award for best world music album. Serious Tam followed in 2000, Kambek in 2002, Amette in 2004 and Akave in 2010, among others. Abebe is on the 1997 album.

His music combines traditional singing from the islands with guitars and contemporary production. The three-part singing gives the songs a warm, layered sound. For pop history Telek is an example of how local singing traditions from the Pacific reached a worldwide audience through collaborations with Australian musicians.
artiest/george-telek.listen: Listen to Abebe and notice how the voices sing together in three lines. Can you follow the individual voices, and what do the guitars underneath add?

artiest/george-wein.text:
George Wein was an American jazz promoter, pianist and producer, born on 3 October 1925 in Lynn, Massachusetts and died on 13 September 2021. His father was an ear, nose and throat doctor, and his mother played amateur piano. Wein began piano at eight, formed his first jazz band in high school and studied at Boston University. After his army service in the Second World War he graduated in 1950. He then opened the jazz club Storyville in Boston, which later gave its name to a record label. He also taught the history of jazz.

In 1954 Louis and Elaine Lorillard asked him to organise a festival in their home town of Newport, Rhode Island. It was the first open-air jazz festival in the United States and became an annual tradition. Wein also founded the Newport Folk Festival, together with Pete Seeger and Theodore Bikel, and played an important part in the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival and the Playboy Jazz Festival in Los Angeles. In the 1960s he started Festival Productions, which organised major jazz events.

Wein came up with the corporate sponsor at festivals: his Schlitz Salute to Jazz and Kool Jazz Festival were the first jazz events with a sponsor in the title. As a pianist, too, he made records, such as Wein, Women and Song from 1955 and Tribute to Count Basie from 1974. Among other honours he received the French Légion d'honneur and was made Commandeur de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres. His work ensured that jazz became a fixture of the summer festival season.
artiest/george-wein.listen: Listen to Tribute to Count Basie from 1974 and notice Wein's piano playing. He was above all an organiser, but he also played the piano himself.

artiest/georges-auric.text: Georges Auric was a member of Les Six and a friend of Jean Cocteau. For Cocteau he wrote Le sang d'un poète (1930), La belle et la bête (1946) and Orphée (1950). In La belle et la bête he used choir and orchestra for a fairy-tale, dreamlike sound. After the war Auric was also in demand in England. For the Ealing studios he wrote the music for comedies such as Passport to Pimlico (1949) and The Lavender Hill Mob (1951). There he sounds light, fast and witty. He also wrote for the American film Roman Holiday (1953), which was shot in Rome. In this way he linked the French avant-garde with British popular film.
artiest/georges-auric.listen: Compare the floating choir and rich harmonies of the Cocteau films with the brisk, comic orchestration of the Ealing comedies.

artiest/georges-brassens.text:
Georges Brassens was born in 1921 in Sète, in the south of France, the son of a French father and an Italian mother. His mother was very fond of songs. His father and grandfather were bricklayers. In 1943, during the German occupation, he was sent to Germany as a forced labourer. When he was given leave, he did not go back. He found shelter with Jeanne, a hospitable Breton woman with whom he would live for years, and in that time he wrote many songs without earning anything from them.

Brassens saw himself as a writer and composer, not as a singer. In early 1952 the singer Patachou heard him. She found his songs so personal that he had to sing them himself, and she let him perform in her cabaret. Within a short time he was famous. A long series of records followed, with songs such as La Mauvaise Réputation, Chanson pour l'Auvergnat, Les Copains d'abord and Le Gorille. He also set poems to music by, among others, Victor Hugo, Paul Verlaine, François Villon and Louis Aragon.

Brassens accompanied himself on guitar. The melodies seem simple, but the chords are rich and refined. His lyrics are poetic and contrary at the same time: he mocked bourgeois conventions and did not mince his words. That is why some songs were banned from the radio. He is regarded as one of the greatest French poets of the postwar period. With Jacques Brel he became a model for songwriters outside France. He died in 1981.
artiest/georges-brassens.listen: Listen to La Mauvaise Réputation and notice how sparse the accompaniment is: a guitar and a voice, with the emphasis on the words. Hear how he mocks the respectable citizens, who do not like anyone who chooses a different path.

artiest/georges-delerue.text: Georges Delerue from Roubaix studied at the Paris Conservatoire, among others with Darius Milhaud. He became the most important composer of the nouvelle vague. For François Truffaut he wrote Tirez sur le pianiste (1960), Jules et Jim (1962) and La nuit américaine (1973). For Jean-Luc Godard he made Le mépris (1963). The theme of Camille in that film is a slow, repeating string melody that Godard used again and again. Delerue wrote lyrically and melodiously, often for a small ensemble or string orchestra, sometimes in Baroque style. From the 1980s he also worked a great deal in Hollywood. In 1980 he won an Oscar for A Little Romance.
artiest/georges-delerue.listen: Notice the long, melancholy string melody that keeps repeating and so carries the mood of a whole film.

artiest/georgie-fame.text:
Georgie Fame, born Clive Powell on 26 June 1943 in Leigh, Lancashire, is an English R&B and jazz musician. He had piano lessons from the age of seven, worked briefly in a cotton mill after school and played piano in a band in the evenings. After a singing contest at Butlins in Pwllheli he found work with Rory Blackwell. At sixteen he went to London, where on the advice of Lionel Bart he signed a contract with the manager Larry Parnes. Parnes gave him his new name. Fame played piano in Billy Fury's backing band, the Blue Flames, who carried on at the end of 1961 as Georgie Fame and the Blue Flames.

Fame was influenced by jazz, blues, Mose Allison and Willie Mabon, and was one of the first white musicians to be influenced by ska. In the early 1960s he regularly played with the band at the Flamingo Club in London. There he heard Green Onions by Booker T. and the M.G.'s and bought a Hammond organ the next day. In 1963 the band recorded the album Rhythm and Blues at the Flamingo, and the follow-up Fame at Last from 1964 reached number 15 in the UK albums chart.

Fame is the only British act with three number 1 hits as his only top ten entries: Yeh Yeh in 1964, Get Away in 1966 and The Ballad of Bonnie and Clyde in 1968. He continues to perform, often with contemporaries such as Alan Price, Van Morrison and Bill Wyman. Bill Wyman once called him an incredibly good pianist and singer. Fame is an example of a British musician who brought R&B, jazz and ska together in one sound.
artiest/georgie-fame.listen: Listen to Yeh Yeh from 1964 and notice the way of singing. He was influenced by jazz, blues and ska: try to hear which influence you recognise.

artiest/gerald-moore.text:
Gerald Moore was an English pianist who was known above all as an accompanist to famous musicians. He was born on 30 July 1899 in Watford and died on 13 March 1987. He worked with, among others, Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, Kathleen Ferrier, Elisabeth Schumann, Hans Hotter, Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, Victoria de los Ángeles and Pablo Casals. He also gave talks about music on stage, on the radio and on television, and wrote memoirs and practical guides to the performance of Lieder.

Moore was an unwilling piano pupil, who said himself that his mother had to drag him to the piano. When he was thirteen the family emigrated to Toronto, where he studied with Michael Hambourg. After the latter's death in 1915, Hambourg's son Boris Hambourg took him along as accompanist on a tour of Canada. In Toronto he worked as an organist and as a cinema organist for silent films. His parents sent him back to England, where he had lessons from Mark Hambourg. There he earned his living as an accompanist, and Landon Ronald of the Guildhall School advised him to choose that profession. In 1921 he made his first recording, with the violinist Renée Chemet.

Moore preferred singers to instrumentalists and in the early 1920s often recorded with Peter Dawson. Later he became an established name in the song repertoire. His albums include Winterreise from 1955 and 1968, Goethe-Lieder 1 from 1960 and Spanisches Liederbuch from 1967. He showed that an accompanist is an equal partner of the singer.
artiest/gerald-moore.listen: Listen to a recording of Schubert's Winterreise with Gerald Moore at the piano and notice how the piano follows the singer. Try to hear where the piano itself tells something, without the voice.

artiest/gerard-grisey.text:
Gérard Grisey was a French composer of contemporary classical music, born on 17 June 1946 in Belfort and died on 11 November 1998 in Paris, at the age of fifty-two, of a ruptured aneurysm. His first instrument was the accordion, which he was given at the age of five. At nine he had already written an essay about music. He won the Prix de Rome and from 1972 to 1974 stayed at the Villa Medici in Rome. There he became friends with Tristan Murail, with whom in 1973 he founded the group L'Itinéraire, together with Roger Tessier and Michaël Lévinas. In 1974 and 1975 he studied acoustics.

Grisey is regarded as a pioneer of spectral music, a movement that he is said to have founded together with Murail, although he himself later rejected the label. Partiels from 1975, here in the performance by the Asko Ensemble, is one of his best-known pieces and comes from the series Les Espaces acoustiques. He also wrote, among others, Vortex temporum, Quatre chants pour franchir le seuil and Dérives.

Spectral music takes the natural timbre of a sound, the spectrum of overtones, as the starting point for harmony and form. Instruments and voices play together in such a way that they form one complex sound. For anyone who listens to pop music, Grisey is an example of a composer who treats sound itself as material, as electronic music and ambient also do.
artiest/gerard-grisey.listen: Listen to Partiels and notice how the sound changes slowly: a low note is extended with higher sounds, until a whole emerges that sounds like a single instrument. Can you hear how the piece breathes?

artiest/gerard-presencer.text:
Gerard Presencer is a British jazz trumpeter, born on 12 September 1972 in Watford. He came to the trumpet at the age of nine, after hearing a solo by Roy Eldridge. He names Dizzy Gillespie, Lee Morgan, Freddie Hubbard, Kenny Wheeler, Woody Shaw and Clifford Brown as his early influences. At eleven he became the youngest member of the National Youth Jazz Orchestra. At eighteen he was already playing in the groups of the pianist Stan Tracey, including at a concert at the Queen Elizabeth Hall in London that was later released on Blue Note.

Presencer worked with British jazz musicians such as Peter King, John Dankworth, Ronnie Scott and Norma Winstone, and with Americans such as Johnny Griffin, Chris Potter and Herbie Hancock. He plays in Charlie Watts's jazz groups and was the soloist on Cantaloop by US3, the best-selling Blue Note album of the 1990s. Under his own name he made albums such as Platypus, The Optimist and Chasing Reality. He also played as a session musician on records by Sting, Jamiroquai, Zero 7, James Brown, Ray Charles and Joni Mitchell. The score of the computer game L.A. Noire, which won a BAFTA, also contains his trumpet solos.

Since 2010 he has been a member of the Danish Radio Big Band and lives in Copenhagen. Presencer was also a leading teacher: from 1999 to 2010 he headed the jazz department of the Royal Academy of Music and wrote a book on trumpet playing in improvised music. In this way he links the world of jazz with that of pop.
artiest/gerard-presencer.listen: Listen to Cantaloop by US3 and notice the trumpet solo above the hip hop beat. Hear how a jazz solo and a hip hop rhythm reinforce one another there.

artiest/gerhard-behles.text:
Gerhard Behles is a German music entrepreneur and electronic musician who is best known as a co-founder of Ableton. In 1999 he started that company in Berlin together with Robert Henke, with whom he also forms the group Monolake, and the software engineer Bernd Roggendorf. Behles had previously worked on granular synthesis for Native Instruments' Reaktor software and on programs of his own on a Silicon Graphics workstation at the Technische Universität Berlin. He is still the chief executive of Ableton.

From that work came Ableton Live, which appeared as a commercial program in 2001. Live is a digital audio workstation built so that music can not only be made but also played live. Later came the controller Push and the synthesizer Operator, which were used by, among others, Skrillex and Monolake. The company worked with Cycling '74, the makers of Max/MSP, and acquired that firm in 2017.

For pop history Behles matters because of his tools. Live turned the studio from an expensive room full of equipment into a laptop, and gave producers in techno, hip hop and pop the same possibilities on stage as at home. A great deal of contemporary electronic music has been made with his software.
artiest/gerhard-behles.listen: Listen to a recent electronic production and notice how loops and sounds slide over one another in layers. That is also how Ableton Live works: a rhythm to which you can keep adding or taking away while the music carries on.

artiest/geri-halliwell.text:
Geri Halliwell was born in 1972 in Watford, north of London, the daughter of a Spanish mother and an English father. She grew up in a working-class neighbourhood. Before her music career she worked as a dancer in nightclubs in Majorca, as a presenter on Turkish television and as a model. In 1994 she answered an advertisement in the magazine The Stage, which was looking for members for a new girl group. After a few changes the group that would later be called the Spice Girls came together.

In 1996 the debut album Spice appeared. The first single, Wannabe, went to number 1 in 37 countries, and Say You'll Be There, 2 Become 1, Who Do You Think You Are and Mama also reached number one in England. The success was compared with Beatlemania. Because of her red hair Halliwell was nicknamed Ginger Spice. She in particular became associated with the slogan girl power, and her Union Jack dress at the 1997 Brit Awards became an image of that time. In 1998 she left the group.

As a solo artist she had number 1 hits in England with Mi Chico Latino, Lift Me Up, Bag It Up and It's Raining Men (2001), a cover of The Weather Girls. After that she became known above all as a judge on talent shows and as an author of children's books. Later she took part again in Spice Girls reunions. The group showed how a carefully assembled pop group with a strong image and a clear message could conquer the world.
artiest/geri-halliwell.listen: Listen to Wannabe by the Spice Girls and notice how the five voices alternate. Hear how each member gets a line of her own for a moment, so that you hear the group's different personalities in the music too.

artiest/germaine-tailleferre.text: Germaine Tailleferre was the only woman in Les Six. She is best known for her chamber music and piano works, but she also wrote music for dozens of films. In the 1930s she worked with the director Maurice Cloche and wrote music for a series of documentaries. After the war came, among others, Coïncidences (1947) and Les grandes personnes (1961). Her film music is clear and light, with a French neoclassical tone: distinct melodies, transparent accompaniment and few heavy effects. Most of her film work remained unpublished and has therefore hardly been recorded. What you can hear now is mainly piano arrangements of excerpts. Her career shows how, in France, even concert composers began writing for the cinema from the early days of sound film.
artiest/germaine-tailleferre.listen: Notice the clear, neoclassical melodic lines and the simple accompaniment, here in a piano version.

artiest/gerry-goffin.text:
Gerry Goffin was born on 11 February 1939 in Brooklyn and grew up in Queens, New York. As a boy he already made up lyrics in his head, as a game. After a year at the naval academy he went to study chemistry at Queens College. There he met Carol Klein, who wrote songs under the name Carole King. She wrote the music, he the lyrics. In 1959 they married, and shortly afterwards they both signed a contract with the music publisher Aldon in Manhattan.

The breakthrough came with Will You Love Me Tomorrow, which The Shirelles took to number 1 in America in January 1961. A long series of hits for others followed: Take Good Care of My Baby for Bobby Vee, The Loco-Motion for Little Eva, Up on the Roof for The Drifters, One Fine Day for The Chiffons, (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman for Aretha Franklin and Pleasant Valley Sunday for The Monkees. John Lennon said in 1963 that he and Paul McCartney wanted to become the Goffin-King of England.

After his divorce from King, Goffin worked with other composers, such as Michael Masser. With him he wrote Theme from Mahogany (Do You Know Where You're Going To) and Saving All My Love for You, which both reached number 1. In all he wrote more than a hundred hits on the American Billboard Hot 100. His gift, according to others, was that he found words for what many young people felt but could not say. In 1990 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with King. He died on 19 June 2014.
artiest/gerry-goffin.listen: Listen to Will You Love Me Tomorrow by The Shirelles (1960). Notice Goffin's lyrics: a girl wonders whether tonight's love will still exist tomorrow, a doubt that is voiced honestly and without ado.

artiest/gerry-mulligan.text: Gerry Mulligan was a baritone saxophonist and arranger. As a young man he wrote for big bands and for the nonet of Birth of the Cool. In 1952 he started a quartet without piano in Los Angeles, with the trumpeter Chet Baker. Without a piano the two horns could play freely against each other, while bass and drums marked the harmony and the rhythm. The quartet became very popular and defined the image of West Coast jazz. Mulligan played the big, low baritone saxophone lightly and nimbly. Later he led his Concert Jazz Band and played with Thelonious Monk and Astor Piazzolla. He often performed in Europe, including at the North Sea Jazz Festival.
artiest/gerry-mulligan.listen: Hear how the low baritone and the high trumpet circle around one another.

artiest/gerry-mulligan-quartet.text:
The Gerry Mulligan Quartet was a quartet built around the American baritone saxophonist Gerry Mulligan. He was born on 6 April 1927 in Queens in New York and died on 20 January 1996. Besides being a saxophonist he was a clarinettist, pianist, composer and arranger, and he was also called Jeru. He grew up in a family that moved often, including to Ohio and Michigan, and began on the clarinet. His baritone sounded light and airy, in the era of Cool Jazz.

In 1952 the album Gerry Mulligan Quartet appeared, with the trumpeter Chet Baker. The line-up had no piano, so that the horns had a great deal of room to play with one another. More recordings followed in the years 1953 to 1955, including Gene Norman Presents the Gerry Mulligan Quartet from 1954 and a record with Lee Konitz. In 1988 Reunion with Chet Baker appeared. My Funny Valentine with Chet Baker, from 1952, is one of the best-known recordings.

The music is calm, clear and transparent. Two melodic lines, baritone sax and trumpet, weave around each other over a rhythm section of bass and drums, and the sound is soft rather than sharp. The quartet became one of the best-known examples of Cool Jazz on the American West Coast. It showed that jazz could also sound restrained, almost like chamber music, and influenced many later small groups.
artiest/gerry-mulligan-quartet.listen: Listen to My Funny Valentine and follow the trumpet of Chet Baker and the baritone sax in turn. Notice that there is no piano: can you hear how the open space between the instruments lets the melody float?

artiest/gers-pardoel.text:
Gerwin Pardoel, Gers for short, is a Dutch rapper from Nijmegen, born on 12 May 1981. He grew up in a family where his mother died when he was seventeen, and he then sought support above all in inline skating. Later in Rotterdam he became friends with the rapper Postman, who introduced him to hip hop and helped with his stage name: in Rotterdam dialect gers means something like cool. Postman had a great influence on his way of performing.

In 2009 he broke through with Broodje Bakpao, a collaboration with The Opposites that became the title song of the film New Kids Turbo and reached number one on the Mega Single Top 100. His debut album Deze wereld is van jou appeared in 2011 and went platinum in the Netherlands. From it Ik neem je mee became an enormous hit: the song topped the Top 40 and, on the basis of the points system, became the biggest Dutch-language hit ever in that chart. Bagagedrager, with Sef, was also a great success in the Netherlands and Belgium. De toekomst is van ons, Voor m'n kids and Juli followed later.

Pardoel raps in Dutch, with melodic choruses and light-hearted lyrics about everyday life. In doing so he belonged to Nederhop, which in the years after 2000 grew from the underground into the charts. His success in Flanders also brought him onto television, including as a coach on The Voice Kids.
artiest/gers-pardoel.listen: Listen to Ik neem je mee and notice how the chorus is singable, while the verse is rapped. Hear how that mix makes a rap song accessible to a wide audience.

artiest/gershon-kingsley.text:
Gershon Kingsley was born in 1922 as Götz Gustav Ksinski in Bochum and grew up in Berlin. Because his father was Jewish, he fled in 1938, a few days before Kristallnacht, to a kibbutz in what was then Palestine. There he taught himself to play the piano. He played jazz in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem and studied at the Jerusalem conservatoire. After the Second World War he emigrated to America, where he became a conductor of Broadway musicals.

In the 1960s Kingsley worked as an arranger at Vanguard Records. There, with the French musician Jean-Jacques Perrey, he formed the duo Perrey and Kingsley, who released The In Sound from Way Out! (1966) and Kaleidoscopic Vibrations (1967). In 1969 he released the album Music to Moog By, with arrangements of music by, among others, The Beatles and Beethoven, and pieces of his own. It included Popcorn, the track that made him famous. In 1970 his First Moog Quartet became the first group to play electronic music at Carnegie Hall.

Kingsley was one of the pioneers of the Moog synthesizer. He showed that this new instrument was suited not only to experiments but also to cheerful, catchy pop music. His work ranged from avant-garde to advertising music, and he also wrote rock-style music for Jewish celebrations. Later he worked with the first digital synthesizers, such as the Fairlight and the Synclavier. He died in 2019 in New York, aged 97.
artiest/gershon-kingsley.listen: Listen to Popcorn and notice the short, bouncy synthesizer notes that give the track its name. Hear how one simple melody is repeated again and again, while little sounds are added around it.

artiest/gesang.text:
Gesang Martohartono was a Javanese singer and songwriter from Surakarta, also called Solo, in Central Java. He was born on 1 October 1917 and died on 20 May 2010. His father had a batik business that went bankrupt when Gesang was a teenager, after which the family fell into poverty. He was self-taught and could not read music. To support his family he wrote songs and sang at local celebrations.

In 1940, shortly before the Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies, the twenty-three-year-old composed, with the help of a flute, a melody in kroncong, an urban musical form of the region that combined Javanese chord patterns with Western-sounding singing. For the lyrics he was inspired by the Bengawan Solo, the longest and most important river of Java, which for him symbolised the endurance of Javanese culture. Bengawan Solo became popular among the Javanese and became known nationwide through the radio. Japanese soldiers, too, grew fond of the song during the occupation.

When the soldiers returned home after the war, they took the song with them to Japan. In the dark time after the defeat it matched the mood of the public, and best-selling recordings made it known across the country. Versions appeared in other Asian countries, and artists all over the world have since performed it anew. The song is regarded as almost synonymous with kroncong.
artiest/gesang.listen: Listen to Bengawan Solo and notice the calm, swaying accompaniment and the simple, singing melody. Try humming the line along: why does it stick so easily?

artiest/geto-boys.text:
The Geto Boys were an American rap group from Houston, Texas. The group began in 1986 under the name Ghetto Boys, with, among others, DJ Ready Red and the dancer who later became Bushwick Bill. Their first single was Car Freak in 1986, and their debut album Making Trouble followed in 1988. It attracted little attention and the group split up, after which a new line-up formed. The best-known line-up consisted of Bushwick Bill, Willie D and Scarface.

Their breakthrough came with the albums Grip It! On That Other Level from 1989 and We Can't Be Stopped from 1991. The latter contains Mind Playing Tricks on Me, their biggest hit, which reached number twenty-three on the Billboard Hot 100. The cover shows Bushwick Bill, who had lost an eye in a shooting, in a hospital bed. Till Death Do Us Part, The Resurrection and Da Good da Bad & da Ugly followed, among others. The group remained active until Bushwick Bill died in 2019.

The lyrics dealt with violence, sex, mental health problems and addiction, but also with police violence and the consequences of violence in the city. In doing so the Geto Boys pushed gangsta rap to the limit, and politicians in the United States sharply criticised them for it. Their soulful sound put Houston on the hip hop map and later inspired artists such as 2Pac, Eminem, UGK and T.I.
artiest/geto-boys.listen: Listen to Mind Playing Tricks on Me and notice the sombre, calm beat and how the three rappers each tell a verse of their own about fear and suspicion. Hear how soft the track sounds, while the lyrics are so dark.

artiest/getty-kaspers.text:
Getty Kaspers is a Dutch singer, born on 5 March 1948 in Graz in Austria, the daughter of a Dutch mother and an Austrian father. She grew up in a foster family in Austria and later came to the Netherlands. In Enschede she came into contact with the band Teach-In through the bass guitarist Johnny Gaasbeek, and in the early 1970s she became its singer. In 1974 the group had three hits in the Dutch top fifteen, including In The Summernight, which reached number three in the Netherlands and Belgium.

The big moment came in 1975. Teach-In won the Dutch heat for the Eurovision Song Contest with Ding-a-dong, and Kaspers opened the final in Stockholm. The group won the contest with 152 points. Ding-a-dong then reached number three in the Dutch Top 40 and number thirteen in Great Britain, and another big hit followed with Goodbye Love. When the album Get On Board and the single Rose Valley disappointed, Teach-In broke up in 1978. Kaspers carried on solo under the name Getty, recorded the Getty Album and briefly sang in the trio Balloon.

The group made a fresh start without her, but in 2009 she performed with the original line-up at the opening of the Song Contest in Moscow. Her story shows how in the 1970s the Song Contest was a springboard for European pop music, with simple, cheerful songs that everyone could sing along to.
artiest/getty-kaspers.listen: Listen to Ding-a-dong and notice the chorus with its short, repeated sounds. Hear how such a simple melody sticks almost immediately.

artiest/giacomo-puccini.text:
Giacomo Puccini was born on 22 December 1858 in Lucca, into a family that had for generations directed the church music of the city. His father died when he was still a child. After a short career as an organist he decided to become an opera composer, having seen a performance of Verdi's Aïda. He studied at the Milan conservatoire and with Le Villi in 1884 got his first opera onto the stage. His breakthrough came with Manon Lescaut in 1893.

The works followed that kept him famous: La bohème in 1896, Tosca in 1900 and Madama Butterfly in 1904. Madama Butterfly received a hostile reception at its first performance in Milan, but was revised afterwards. His last opera, Turandot, remained unfinished; Franco Alfano completed it after his death in 1924. These four operas are among the most performed and recorded in the entire repertoire.

Puccini is regarded as the greatest and most successful continuer of Italian opera after Verdi. His music is richly orchestrated and builds on melodies that grip you directly. In Tosca he used fixed musical hallmarks for certain characters, which reminded some of Wagner. His operatic melodies later returned again and again in film, advertising and pop music, and recordings of his work appear on many albums by great singers and conductors.
artiest/giacomo-puccini.listen: Listen to an aria from La bohème and notice how the singing voice rises above the orchestra. Hear how the melody carries you into the emotion of the moment.

artiest/gil-evans.text: Gil Evans was born in Toronto and taught himself to arrange by listening to records by Duke Ellington. In the 1940s he wrote for Claude Thornhill's orchestra, with horns and tuba and long, floating chords. His small apartment in New York became a meeting place for young musicians, and there the plan for the nonet of Birth of the Cool took shape. With Miles Davis he made, among other things, three albums for large orchestra: Miles Ahead (1957), Porgy and Bess (1958) and Sketches of Spain (1960). Evans wrote tone colours with flutes, horns and tubas that recall classical music rather than a big band. Later his orchestra also played music by Jimi Hendrix.
artiest/gil-evans.listen: Listen to the soft, strange harmonies of horns, flutes and tubas.

artiest/gil-fuller.text:
Walter Gilbert Fuller, better known as Gil Fuller, was an American jazz arranger. He was born on 14 April 1920 in Los Angeles and died on 26 May 1994 in San Diego. He studied in New York and then returned to the West Coast, where he became an arranger for Les Hite. Later he wrote for Jimmie Lunceford and Tiny Bradshaw, and after Billy Eckstine formed his orchestra in 1944, Fuller became his arranger.

In the 1930s and 1940s he wrote parts for many well-known bandleaders, including Benny Carter, Benny Goodman, Woody Herman and Count Basie. He also worked for Machito and Tito Puente. After the Second World War he was increasingly in demand as an arranger of bebop, in the same circle as Tadd Dameron, Gil Evans and George Russell. He wrote for Dizzy Gillespie's big band, and in 1965 the album Gil Fuller and the Monterey Jazz Festival Orchestra Featuring Dizzy Gillespie appeared.

In 1957 Fuller started a music publishing company of his own. He continued to work for jazz musicians, among them Stan Kenton, and also began writing for film and pop, including for Ray Charles. An arranger seldom appears on the sleeve, but his work determines how an orchestra sounds. Fuller helped translate bebop to the large orchestra.
artiest/gil-fuller.listen: Listen to the 1965 album with the Monterey Jazz Festival Orchestra and Dizzy Gillespie. Notice how the horns answer Gillespie's trumpet as a group.

artiest/gilbert-o-sullivan.text:
Gilbert O'Sullivan, really Raymond Edward O'Sullivan, is an Irish singer-songwriter, born on 1 December 1946 in Waterford. As a child he moved with his family to Swindon in England, where he studied graphic design and played in amateur bands. In 1967 he moved to London to become a musician. To stand out he devised a striking look with a pudding-basin haircut, a cap and short trousers, inspired by his love of silent film. His first singles had no success.

The breakthrough came at the end of 1970 with Nothing Rhymed, a hit in England and the Netherlands. In 1972 came international stardom with Alone Again (Naturally), a ballad about loss and suicide that spent six weeks at number one in America. Clair and Get Down followed, from the album I'm a Writer, Not a Fighter from 1973. In 1972 Record Mirror named him England's best male singer, and in 1973 he received an Ivor Novello Award. His record contract with the label MAM later led to a lawsuit, which he won in 1982.

His music stands out for his pounding piano playing and his lyrical jokes and observations. His name is also linked with the music rights of hip hop. In 1991 he won a lawsuit against the rapper Biz Markie, who had sampled a piece of Alone Again (Naturally) without permission. Since then hip hop makers have had to have samples cleared.
artiest/gilbert-o-sullivan.listen: Listen to Alone Again (Naturally) and notice the calm piano and the soft voice. Hear how light the song sounds, while the lyrics are about sorrow.

artiest/giles-martin.text:
Giles Martin is an English producer, composer and multi-instrumentalist, born on 9 October 1969. He is the son of George Martin, the Beatles' producer. His first group was called Velvet Jones, and at university he wrote jingles. As a teenager he worked for his father, whose hearing had been deteriorating since the mid-1970s. Giles himself said of this that he became his father's ears at a young age.

As a producer he worked with, among others, Kula Shaker, Jeff Beck, Elvis Costello, INXS, Kate Bush, Elton John and the Rolling Stones. In 2004 he made Pure by Hayley Westenra, the fastest-selling classical album ever in Great Britain. His name remained linked above all with the Beatles. In 2006 he made Love with his father, the music for a Cirque du Soleil show in Las Vegas, in which Beatles songs were mixed with digital techniques into a new whole. For this he received two Grammys. He also worked on The Beatles: Rock Band in 2009 and on new recordings by Paul McCartney in 2013. In 2022 he won an Emmy for The Beatles: Get Back.

Since 2014 he has been responsible for sound at Sonos, and since 2018 he has been head of audio at Universal Music Group at Abbey Road Studios. In this way he ensures that old recordings are heard anew with modern means.
artiest/giles-martin.listen: Listen to a new mix of a Beatles song that Giles Martin worked on and compare it with the old one. Notice how the voices and instruments now have more room.

artiest/gilles-peterson.text:
Gilles Peterson, born Gilles Jérôme Moehrle on 28 September 1964, is a British DJ, broadcaster and label boss. He grew up in the soul scene of south London and as a teenager was already playing on pirate radio stations. In 1986 and 1987 he presented Mad on Jazz on BBC Radio London and became known as a DJ of acid jazz, a mixture of jazz, funk, Latin and Brazilian music from the 1970s. In 1990 he was there at the start of Jazz FM, but he was sacked because he played anti-war music during the first Gulf War.

Afterwards he worked at Kiss FM and from 1998 at BBC Radio 1 with his programme Worldwide, in which he linked different styles together. In 2012 he moved to BBC Radio 6 Music. In 1988 he started the label Acid Jazz and then founded Talkin' Loud, where Roni Size with Reprazent won the Mercury Prize in 1997 for New Forms. In 2006 he started Brownswood Recordings and the Worldwide Festival in Sète.

Peterson takes jazz as his starting point, but also plays dance music and music from all over the world. He shows how a DJ does not simply play records, but also connects people and scenes and gives new talent a platform.
artiest/gilles-peterson.listen: Listen to New Forms by Roni Size and Reprazent, released on Talkin' Loud. Notice how the drums and the acoustic bass link jazz and drum and bass.

artiest/ginger-baker.text:
Ginger Baker's real name was Peter Baker, and he was born in 1939 in Lewisham, in south London. He got his nickname from his flaming red hair. His father was killed in 1943 in the Second World War. Around the age of fifteen he began drumming, and in the early 1960s he took lessons from Phil Seamen, one of the best British jazz drummers. He played in Blues Incorporated and the Graham Bond Organisation, both times with the bassist Jack Bruce, with whom he was constantly quarrelling.

Nevertheless, in 1966 Baker and Bruce formed Cream together with the guitarist Eric Clapton. The trio mixed blues with psychedelic rock and hard rock and made four albums in a little over two years. In 1968 the group broke up, partly because of the clashes between Baker and Bruce. Afterwards he played with Clapton and Steve Winwood in Blind Faith and started Ginger Baker's Air Force. In the 1970s he travelled across the Sahara to Nigeria, where he set up a studio in Lagos and played with Fela Kuti. Later he played with, among others, Hawkwind and Public Image Ltd.

Baker brought jazz and African rhythms into rock and is sometimes called the first superstar among rock drummers. He played with two bass drums instead of one, after the example of the jazz drummer Louie Bellson. In the Cream song Toad he played a long drum solo, one of the first on a rock record. His life was wild and often self-destructive, and his short temper made long collaborations difficult. In 2016 Rolling Stone put him third among the best drummers of all time. He died in 2019.
artiest/ginger-baker.listen: Listen to Toad by Cream and notice Ginger Baker's drum solo. Hear how he builds ever new rhythms with two bass drums and his tom-toms, more like a jazz drummer than an ordinary rock drummer.
